title: Visual defect detection for manufacturing
tagline: A YOLO detector fine-tuned on steel surface defects, exported to ONNX and served on CPU with a review screen for the quality inspector.
pitch: I built a visual inspection system that looks at a photo of a steel surface, draws a box around every defect, names the defect type and tells the inspector whether the part passes, needs a second look or is rejected. I fine-tuned a small YOLO model on a public dataset of 1,797 labelled steel images, measured it on images it never saw, and exported it so that it runs on an ordinary CPU with no graphics card and no deep learning framework installed. The inspector gets a review screen where every decision can be confirmed or corrected, and those corrections are saved as new training data.
problem: A steel plant, or any factory with a surface to inspect, checks parts by eye. People get tired, two inspectors disagree, and a defect that slips through is paid for later as a customer return. Cameras are cheap, but the plant needs software that finds the defect, says what kind it is, runs on the modest computer already next to the line, and is honest about how often it is wrong.
solution: A small object detection model (YOLO11 nano) is fine-tuned on the public NEU steel surface defect dataset, which has six defect types with a box drawn around each defect. The trained model is exported to the ONNX format and run with ONNX Runtime, so the serving side needs no PyTorch and works on a CPU. Around the model there is a decision layer that turns boxes into a verdict (pass, review, reject), an evaluation script that measures the exported model on held-out images, and a review screen plus a JSON API for the inspector and for other systems.
features: Finds and names six steel surface defect types, with a box and a confidence for each one
Runs on CPU with ONNX Runtime only: no PyTorch and no graphics card on the serving machine
Turns detections into a verdict for the inspector: pass, review or reject
Review screen where the inspector confirms or corrects each result, saved as a log for retraining
JSON API so a line controller or another system can send an image and get the detections back
Evaluation on held-out images: accuracy per defect type, missed defects, false alarms and speed
A classical OpenCV baseline, measured the same way, to show what the trained model adds
ONNX export verified box for box against the original PyTorch model

stack.name: Ultralytics YOLO11n
stack.role: The detection model and the training loop used for fine-tuning.
stack.why: The nano model has about 2.6 million parameters, so it trains and runs on a CPU. Larger models or transformer detectors would need a graphics card to train in reasonable time.

stack.name: ONNX Runtime
stack.role: Runs the exported model in production.
stack.why: It is a small runtime that needs no PyTorch, so the serving install is light and the model can later move to a C++, .NET or edge device without retraining.

stack.name: OpenCV
stack.role: Reads images, resizes them for the model, draws the boxes, and powers the classical baseline.
stack.why: It is the standard image library, fast on CPU, and already present on most industrial vision computers.

stack.name: Gradio
stack.role: The review screen for the inspector.
stack.why: It gives image upload, an annotated result and a feedback form in a few lines of Python, which is enough for a review tool; a custom React front end would add work without adding proof.

stack.name: FastAPI
stack.role: The JSON endpoint for other systems, and the host for the review screen.
stack.why: It validates input, documents the API automatically and serves the Gradio screen in the same process, so there is one command to run.

stack.name: pytest
stack.role: Automated tests for the geometry, the metrics, the detector and the API.
stack.why: It is the standard Python test runner and the tests run offline.

workflow.detail: A photo of the surface arrives from the review screen, the API or the command line. It is decoded with OpenCV.
The image is resized to the model's input size with padding so its shape is not distorted, and the pixel values are scaled to the range 0 to 1.
ONNX Runtime runs the exported YOLO model on the CPU. The model returns several thousand candidate boxes, each with a score for each of the six defect types.
Candidates below the confidence threshold are dropped, overlapping boxes for the same defect are merged (non-maximum suppression), and box coordinates are mapped back to the original image.
A rule turns the remaining boxes into a verdict: no box means pass, a confident box means reject, and a low-confidence box means the inspector should look.
The inspector sees the image with boxes and the verdict, confirms it or corrects it, and the answer is appended to a review log that becomes training data for the next model version.

phases.name: Foundation
phases.goal: A repository with the public dataset downloaded, converted and split, the scoring code written, and a classical baseline measured.

steps.text: Create the repository skeleton, the configuration and the pinned requirements
Write the download script that fetches the NEU steel defect dataset at a fixed revision
Convert the Pascal VOC annotations to YOLO format and check every box
Split the images into train, validation and test sets with a fixed seed, balanced by defect type
Write the detection metrics (IoU, average precision, mAP) with tests
Measure a classical OpenCV baseline that finds defects without any training

phases.outcome: The repository has the NEU steel defect dataset downloaded at a pinned version and converted to YOLO labels: 1,257 training, 270 validation and 270 test images with 2,889, 662 and 626 labelled defects. The scoring code (IoU, average precision, mAP, confidence intervals, confusion matrix) is written in NumPy and covered by 21 passing tests. The classical OpenCV baseline, tuned on validation and measured on test, finds defects with an average precision of 0.094 at IoU 0.5 (precision 0.21, recall 0.22), which is the number the trained model has to beat.

phases.name: Model
phases.goal: A YOLO11n model fine-tuned on the training images on CPU and exported to ONNX.

steps.text: Time one training epoch on the CPU and choose image size and number of epochs
Fine-tune YOLO11n from the pretrained weights with a fixed seed
Record the training curve and the validation score
Export the best weights to ONNX

phases.outcome: YOLO11n was fine-tuned for 50 epochs at 320 pixels on the CPU in 81.7 minutes (seed 0). Its best validation score in the training log is mAP 0.714 at IoU 0.5 and 0.408 averaged over IoU 0.5 to 0.95. The best weights were exported to a 10.5 MB ONNX file, model/defects.onnx, with a model card that records the input format, the class list and a checksum. The per-epoch history is in reports/training.json and plotted in docs/training_curve.png.

phases.name: Inference
phases.goal: A detector that runs the ONNX model with ONNX Runtime and OpenCV only, and a rule that turns boxes into a verdict.

steps.text: Write the image preparation (letterbox resize) and its inverse mapping
Decode the model output and apply non-maximum suppression per defect type
Check that the ONNX detector agrees with the PyTorch model on the same images
Write the verdict rule (pass, review, reject) and the drawing of boxes
Add a command line tool that detects defects in one image or a folder

phases.outcome: The detector in defects/detector.py loads the ONNX file with ONNX Runtime and does the resize, decoding and non-maximum suppression itself, with no PyTorch. On 60 validation images it returns the same 107 boxes as the PyTorch model, with a largest confidence difference of 0.0 (reports/parity.json). defects/service.py turns the boxes into a pass, review or reject verdict with one plain sentence of explanation and draws the boxes on the image. The command line tool inspects a file or a folder: on the twelve sample images it answers in 21 to 36 milliseconds each.

phases.name: Evaluation
phases.goal: Honest numbers for the exported model on the held-out test images.

steps.text: Choose the confidence thresholds on the validation set, never on the test set
Measure mAP and per-class precision and recall on the test set with the ONNX model
Add confidence intervals by resampling the test images
Measure CPU latency per image
Produce figures: predictions against ground truth, per-class scores, confusion between classes
Write the evaluation report with the weak spots named

phases.outcome: The exported model was measured on the 270 held-out test images (626 labelled defects) by python -m defects.evaluate. mAP at IoU 0.5 is 0.747 (95 percent interval 0.720 to 0.782) and mAP at 0.5 to 0.95 is 0.413. At the thresholds chosen on validation, it finds 469 of 626 defects (recall 0.75) with 258 false alarms (precision 0.65). Scratches (0.95), patches (0.93), inclusion (0.85) and pitted surface (0.84) are strong; rolled-in scale (0.53) and crazing (0.39) are weak. Of the 270 defective test images, 268 are rejected and 2 pass. Finding a defect regardless of type, the model scores 0.786 against 0.094 for the OpenCV baseline. Median latency is about 21 ms per image on a 2014 Xeon CPU. The report is reports/evaluation.md with figures in docs/.

phases.name: Interface
phases.goal: One command that starts a review screen and a JSON API.

steps.text: Build the JSON endpoint that accepts an image and returns detections and a verdict
Build the review screen with the annotated image, the detection table and the threshold control
Save the inspector's confirmation or correction to a review log
Run the server, call it for real, and take a screenshot

phases.outcome: python -m defects.app starts one server on port 7860. The review screen lets the inspector upload an image or pick an example, shows the boxes, a coloured verdict and a table of detections, has a slider to make the model more or less sensitive, and saves the inspector's judgement and the image to a review log. The JSON API has /api/health, /api/detect and /api/reviews/summary, and refuses empty, oversized and non-image uploads with clear messages. It was started from an environment that contains only the serving requirements (no PyTorch), called with curl, and driven in a headless browser to take docs/screen.png.

phases.name: Verification and documentation
phases.goal: A repository a client can clone, run and trust.

steps.text: Run the full test suite offline
Run the quick start from a clean environment using only the serving requirements
Write the README with the diagram, real output, results and limits
Complete the dashboard entry: decisions, client questions, concepts, keywords
Check for secrets, add the licence, and make the final commit

phases.outcome: The repository is complete: 69 tests pass offline, including in a fresh environment with only the serving requirements and no PyTorch. The README has the architecture diagram, the screenshot, the measured results with intervals, real command output, the API, the retraining steps, the limits and the licence situation of the code, the model and the dataset. The dashboard entry has 9 decisions with alternatives, 13 client questions, 22 concepts and 36 keywords. No secrets are tracked.

decisions.title: Which dataset to train on
decisions.chosen: The public NEU steel surface defect dataset (NEU-DET), in its cleaned release with duplicates removed: 1,797 images, 4,177 labelled boxes, six defect types.
decisions.why: It is a real industrial dataset with boxes drawn by people, it is the standard benchmark for steel surface inspection so my numbers can be compared with published ones, and it is small enough to train on a CPU in about an hour. I used the cleaned release, pinned to one exact version, because the original contains three duplicated images; a duplicate that lands in both the training and the test set makes the test score look better than it is.

alternatives.option: Severstal steel defect dataset
alternatives.why_not: It is larger and closer to a production line, but it is distributed through Kaggle behind a login and a competition agreement, so a stranger could not run my download script, and its 12,000 large images are too slow to train on a CPU.

alternatives.option: MVTec AD
alternatives.why_not: It is built for anomaly detection (learn from good parts only) and its licence forbids commercial use. It answers a different question from the one a client asks when they say YOLO and object detection.

alternatives.option: Synthetic defects drawn by a script
alternatives.why_not: A model that scores well on defects I drew myself proves nothing about real steel.

decisions.at_scale: A real project trains on the client's own images from the client's own camera and lighting. The public dataset is the starting point and the proof of method; I would expect to label a few hundred images per defect type from the real line, and I would agree the dataset licence before anything ships, because the NEU authors state no licence.

decisions.title: How to split the data and what to compare against
decisions.chosen: A fixed 70/15/15 split into training, validation and test images, balanced by defect type, with the image lists committed to the repository. A classical OpenCV method with no training is measured on the same test images as the baseline.
decisions.why: The test images are touched once, at the end. Every setting (training length, confidence thresholds, the baseline's own settings) is chosen on the validation images. Committing the lists means anyone can check which images a number refers to. The baseline matters because a client should see what the trained model adds over a week of classical image processing: the baseline finds defects with an average precision of 0.09.

alternatives.option: The 80/10/10 split published with the dataset
alternatives.why_not: Its test set has 180 images, 30 per defect type. With 270 test images the confidence intervals are noticeably tighter, which matters more to me than matching someone else's split.

alternatives.option: Cross-validation over five folds
alternatives.why_not: It would give a more stable number but needs five training runs of over an hour each on CPU. I report a confidence interval from resampling the test images instead.

alternatives.option: No baseline
alternatives.why_not: A score with nothing to compare it to cannot be judged.

decisions.at_scale: In a plant the split must be by time or by production batch, not random: images from the same coil look alike, and a random split lets the model see near-copies of the test images. The public dataset has no batch information, so I could not do this here.

decisions.title: Which detection model to fine-tune
decisions.chosen: YOLO11n, the smallest model of the Ultralytics YOLO11 family (2.6 million parameters), starting from weights pretrained on the COCO dataset.
decisions.why: The whole project has to train and run on a CPU. The nano model trains in 82 minutes on 8 cores and answers in about 21 milliseconds per image. Starting from pretrained weights matters more than the model size here: 1,257 training images are too few to learn edges and textures from zero, but enough to re-aim a model that already knows them.

alternatives.option: A larger YOLO model (small or medium)
alternatives.why_not: It would probably add a few points of accuracy, but training is three to eight times slower on CPU and the serving latency goes up in proportion. I did not measure it, so I do not claim a number.

alternatives.option: A transformer detector such as RT-DETR
alternatives.why_not: It needs a graphics card to train in reasonable time and is slower on CPU. Its licence is more permissive, which is its real advantage; see the licence decision.

alternatives.option: Anomaly detection trained on good parts only (for example PatchCore)
alternatives.why_not: That is the right tool when there are no labelled defects, but it cannot name the defect type, and this dataset has no defect-free images to learn from.

alternatives.option: Image classification (one label per image)
alternatives.why_not: It does not say where the defect is or how many there are, which the inspector needs in order to check the result.

decisions.at_scale: With a graphics card for training I would compare the nano, small and medium models on the client's images and pick the smallest one that meets the agreed miss rate at the line speed.

decisions.title: Image size and training length
decisions.chosen: Training and inference at 320 by 320 pixels, for 50 epochs, with flips in both directions and brightness changes as augmentation.
decisions.why: The source images are 200 by 200 pixels, so 320 enlarges them by 1.6, which helps with the thin inclusions. I timed one epoch first (about 100 seconds) and set 50 epochs as a budget of roughly an hour and a half. A steel surface has no up or down, so flipping in both directions is valid extra variety; hue and saturation changes are switched off because the images are grey.

alternatives.option: 640 pixels, the YOLO default
alternatives.why_not: Four times the computation per image for a 200 pixel source; there is no extra detail to find.

alternatives.option: Train until the validation score stops improving
alternatives.why_not: The curve was still rising slowly at epoch 50 (validation mAP at 0.5 went from 0.69 at epoch 40 to 0.71 at epoch 50), so more epochs would likely help a little. I stopped at the CPU budget and say so in the limits.

alternatives.option: Search over learning rate and augmentation settings
alternatives.why_not: Each trial costs over an hour on this machine. I kept the library defaults, which are well tested, and spent the time on honest evaluation.

decisions.at_scale: On a graphics card the same run takes a few minutes, so I would train to convergence, run a small search over the settings, and repeat with three seeds to report the spread.

decisions.title: How to run the model in production
decisions.chosen: ONNX Runtime on CPU, with the image preparation and the box clean-up (letterbox resize, decoding, non-maximum suppression) written in this repository with NumPy and OpenCV.
decisions.why: The serving install has no PyTorch and no Ultralytics: I checked this by installing only requirements.txt into an empty environment and running the tests there. That makes the install small, removes the training library from the production machine, and means the same ONNX file can be loaded from C++, C# or an edge device later. I verified the export against PyTorch on 60 validation images: 107 boxes from each, all 107 matched, with identical confidences.

alternatives.option: Serve with the Ultralytics library directly
alternatives.why_not: It is three lines of code, but it pulls PyTorch (hundreds of megabytes) onto the production machine and ties the running service to the AGPL-licensed library.

alternatives.option: OpenVINO
alternatives.why_not: Usually faster than ONNX Runtime on Intel processors, but it only targets Intel hardware. ONNX is the neutral format, and an OpenVINO build can be made from the same file if the line needs more speed.

alternatives.option: TensorRT
alternatives.why_not: It needs an NVIDIA graphics card, which this project deliberately does not assume.

decisions.at_scale: For a camera at line speed I would benchmark OpenVINO and 8-bit quantisation on the actual industrial PC, and batch images if several cameras share one machine.

decisions.title: How to turn boxes into a decision
decisions.chosen: Three outcomes. Reject when at least one box is at or above the confidence threshold of its defect type. Review when there are only weaker boxes above a low floor. Pass when there is nothing above the floor. Each defect type has its own threshold.
decisions.why: A model returns boxes and probabilities; a line needs a decision, and it needs a way to send doubtful parts to a person instead of guessing. One threshold per defect type is necessary because the model's confidence means different things for different types: it is very sure about scratches (threshold 0.45) and never very sure about crazing (threshold 0.08).

alternatives.option: One threshold of 0.25 for everything, the library default
alternatives.why_not: It would drop most crazing detections, whose confidences are low even when they are right, and keep too many weak scratch boxes.

alternatives.option: Reject on any box at all
alternatives.why_not: It gives the inspector no way to tell a clear defect from a doubtful one.

alternatives.option: Rules on defect size and position, as in a real acceptance standard
alternatives.why_not: That is how a plant actually decides (a 2 mm scratch may be fine, a 20 mm one is not), but it needs the client's standard and a pixel-to-millimetre calibration. The rule lives in one function so it can be replaced.

decisions.at_scale: The decision rule would come from the client's quality standard: which defect types matter, at what size, on which zone of the part. The thresholds would be set from the cost of a missed defect against the cost of a false reject, measured on good and bad parts from the line.

decisions.title: How to measure the model
decisions.chosen: My own evaluation script scores the exported ONNX file on the 270 test images, with metrics written in NumPy, thresholds chosen on the validation images only, and a 95 percent confidence interval from resampling the test images 1,000 times.
decisions.why: The number a client should trust is the one measured on the file that ships, through the code that runs in production, not the number the training library printed for its own PyTorch model. Writing the metrics out (about 200 lines, with tests against hand-computed cases) means I can explain exactly what mAP is and can add what the standard tools do not report: the count of missed defects and false alarms at the working thresholds, and what happens per image. The interval matters because 270 images is a small test set: mAP at 0.5 is 0.747, and the honest statement is that it lies between 0.72 and 0.78.

alternatives.option: Report the validation score from the training log
alternatives.why_not: That score was used to pick the best epoch, so it is slightly optimistic, and it measures the PyTorch model, not the exported one.

alternatives.option: Use the pycocotools library
alternatives.why_not: It is the reference implementation and would give nearly the same mAP, but it needs a compiler to install and does not give the per-threshold counts. My implementation follows the same recipe (101 recall points, one match per labelled box).

alternatives.option: Report a single number without an interval
alternatives.why_not: On a test set this small, a difference of two points between two models can be noise. The interval shows that.

decisions.at_scale: I would add a set of good parts to measure the false reject rate, score by production batch to see drift over time, and track the inspector's agreement rate from the review log as the live metric.

decisions.title: What interface to give the inspector and other systems
decisions.chosen: One Python process that serves a Gradio review screen for people and a FastAPI JSON endpoint for machines, started with one command.
decisions.why: The two audiences are different. An inspector needs to see the image with boxes, a clear verdict and a way to say the model was wrong. A line controller or an MES needs to post an image and read JSON. Serving both from one process means one thing to install and start, and both use the same detector and the same thresholds, so they cannot disagree. Every saved review stores the image with the model's answer and the person's judgement: that log is the training data for the next version.

alternatives.option: Streamlit
alternatives.why_not: It is fine for a dashboard but it cannot expose a clean JSON API from the same process, so I would need two services.

alternatives.option: A custom React front end
alternatives.why_not: It would look more polished, but it adds a build step and a second code base without proving anything more about the vision system.

alternatives.option: API only, no screen
alternatives.why_not: A client cannot judge a vision model from JSON. Seeing the boxes on the steel is what makes the result believable, and the review log needs a person in front of a screen.

decisions.at_scale: On a real line the camera would trigger the API directly, results would go to the plant's quality system, the review screen would sit at the inspection station with a login, and reviewed images would flow into a labelling tool and a scheduled retraining job.

decisions.title: How to handle the licence of YOLO and of the dataset
decisions.chosen: Use Ultralytics YOLO for training because it is what clients ask for by name, keep it out of the serving code, and state plainly that the model file is AGPL-3.0 and that the dataset has no stated licence. My own code is MIT.
decisions.why: Ultralytics YOLO is published under AGPL-3.0 and the company states that models trained with it carry that licence. A client who ships a closed product must either buy the Ultralytics Enterprise licence or use another detector. I would rather tell the client this in the first meeting than have their lawyer find it later. Because the data preparation, the metrics, the evaluation, the ONNX serving code and the review screen do not import Ultralytics, swapping the detector means replacing one training script.

alternatives.option: Train with a permissively licensed detector from the start (YOLOX or RT-DETR, both Apache-2.0)
alternatives.why_not: It avoids the question, but clients search for YOLO and Ultralytics is the tool most teams already use. It is the right choice for a closed commercial product without an Enterprise licence, and I say so.

alternatives.option: Say nothing and license everything as MIT
alternatives.why_not: It would be wrong, and it would be the client's legal problem later.

alternatives.option: Do not commit the model file
alternatives.why_not: Then a stranger could not run the project without an 82 minute training run. The file is included, with its licence stated next to it.

decisions.at_scale: Licensing is settled before the first line of code: either the Enterprise licence is budgeted, or the detector is chosen for its licence. The same applies to training data: the client's own images, with clear ownership.

client_qa.q: How accurate is it? Can I trust it on my line?
client_qa.a: On images it never saw, it finds 75 percent of the labelled defects, and its overall detection score (mAP at 0.5) is 0.747. It is strong on four defect types, scratches, patches, inclusions and pitted surface, with scores between 0.84 and 0.95, and weak on two, crazing and rolled-in scale. But these numbers are for a public dataset. On your line, with your camera and your steel, I would expect to retrain on a few hundred of your own labelled images per defect type and measure again before anyone relies on it.

client_qa.q: How many good parts will it wrongly reject? Scrap costs me money.
client_qa.a: I cannot tell you from this dataset, and I would rather say that than invent a number. Every image in the public dataset contains a defect, so there are no good parts to measure false rejects on. What I can say is that at the current settings it raises 258 false boxes across 270 images, half of them on one defect type, crazing. The first thing I would do in a real project is collect images of good parts and set the thresholds from the cost of a false reject against the cost of a missed defect.

On the test set it missed 157 of 626 defects at box level, mostly the two texture-like types: 47 rolled-in scale and 40 crazing. At image level, which is closer to how a plant thinks, 2 of 270 defective images would have passed with nothing flagged. It rarely misses a scratch (7 of 85) or a patch (14 of 123).

client_qa.q: Do I need a GPU or special hardware?
client_qa.a: No. It runs on an ordinary processor in about 21 milliseconds per image, which is around 46 images a second, measured on a desktop Xeon processor from 2014. Training also ran on CPU, in 82 minutes. A graphics card would only make retraining faster. For a high resolution line camera the speed would need measuring again, because those images are much larger.

client_qa.q: How much labelling work is needed for my own defects?
client_qa.a: This model was trained on about 1,250 images with 2,900 boxes, roughly 300 to 700 boxes per defect type. As a rule of thumb I would start with 200 to 300 labelled images per defect type from your line, see where it fails, and add more of those cases. The review screen is built for exactly this: every time the inspector says the model was wrong, the image is saved, and those are the most valuable images to label next.

client_qa.q: Can it connect to our line or our quality system?
client_qa.a: Yes. There is a JSON API: a camera trigger or a PLC gateway posts an image and gets back the verdict, the defect types, the box positions and the confidences. The model is a standard ONNX file, so it can also be loaded directly from C++ or C# on an industrial PC without Python. What is not built here is the plant-specific part: the camera driver, the reject actuator and the link to your MES.

client_qa.q: Isn't this just a YOLO tutorial? What did you actually build?
client_qa.a: Fair question. Training YOLO is twenty lines and I used the library for that. What I built is everything around it that a tutorial skips: a fixed data split with no leakage, the scoring written out and tested so I can explain every number, a classical baseline to show the model is worth it, an export that is verified box for box against the original, serving code with no PyTorch, thresholds per defect type chosen on separate data, a decision rule, a review loop that collects retraining data, and a list of what does not work. The model is the easy tenth.

client_qa.q: Can we use this commercially? What about licences?
client_qa.a: My code is MIT, so yes for the code. Two things need a decision. The YOLO library I trained with is AGPL-3.0 and that licence extends to the trained model, so for a closed product you either buy the Ultralytics Enterprise licence or I retrain with an Apache-licensed detector, which the code is structured to allow. And the public dataset has no stated licence, so a commercial model should be trained on your own images, which it needs anyway.

client_qa.q: Why does the model do so badly on crazing?
client_qa.a: Crazing is a network of fine cracks spread over the whole surface, with no clear edge. The people who labelled the dataset drew the boxes inconsistently: sometimes one big box, sometimes several small ones. The model finds the crazing, but its boxes do not line up with the labelled ones, so the box-overlap score is low. Published results on this dataset show the same pattern. In practice I would treat crazing as a property of the whole image rather than a box.

client_qa.q: What is mAP and why should I care about that number?
client_qa.a: It is the standard score for detectors, between 0 and 1. It checks two things at once: did the model find the defects, and did it avoid false alarms, across all confidence settings. A box counts as correct if it overlaps the labelled box by at least half. I report it because it lets you compare with other systems, but the numbers that matter for a plant are in the same report: how many defects were missed and how many false alarms were raised.

client_qa.q: How do the thresholds work, and can we change them?
client_qa.a: Each defect type has its own confidence threshold, chosen automatically on a separate set of images so that the balance of misses and false alarms is best. A box above the threshold rejects the part; a weaker box sends it to a person. You can change them in one JSON file, override them with one setting, or move a slider in the review screen to make the system more or less sensitive and see the effect immediately.

client_qa.q: What happens when the product or the lighting changes?
client_qa.a: Accuracy will drop, as with any vision model, and the system will not know it by itself. The safeguard built in is the review log: the rate at which the inspector agrees with the model is a live quality signal, and a fall in it means it is time to retrain. The reviewed images are already saved for that. In a real deployment I would add an automatic alert on that rate and a scheduled retraining job.

client_qa.q: How long would a real project take?
client_qa.a: The software here was built in one working session because the data was already labelled. In a real project the time goes into the camera and lighting setup, collecting and labelling images, and agreeing the acceptance rule with quality control. A realistic pilot on one inspection station is a few weeks, most of it data.

concepts.plain: A model that finds things in an image and draws a box around each one, with a name and a confidence. It differs from classification, which gives one label for the whole image and does not say where.
A family of fast object detection models; the name means You Only Look Once, because it finds all boxes in a single pass over the image. YOLO11n is the nano version, the smallest and fastest.

Starting from a model already trained on millions of everyday photos and continuing the training on your own images. The model already knows edges and textures, so a thousand images are enough instead of a million.
The rectangle drawn around a defect, given as the pixel positions of its left, top, right and bottom sides.

A number between 0 and 1 that says how well two boxes overlap: the shared area divided by the total area they cover together. A predicted box usually counts as correct when its IoU with the labelled box is at least 0.5.
Recall is the share of real defects the model found. Precision is the share of the model's boxes that were real defects. Raising the confidence threshold improves precision and lowers recall.

The standard score for detectors, from 0 to 1. For each defect type it summarises precision and recall over all confidence settings, then averages over the types. mAP at 0.5 uses an IoU of 0.5; mAP at 0.5 to 0.95 also demands tighter boxes and is always lower.
The minimum confidence a box needs to be kept. Here each defect type has its own, chosen on validation images, because the model is naturally more sure about some types than others.
The model proposes many overlapping boxes for the same defect. NMS keeps the most confident one and removes the others that overlap it.
Resizing an image to the square size the model expects by scaling it and padding the empty space with grey, instead of stretching it. Stretching would change the shape of the defects.

ONNX is a standard file format for trained models, independent of the tool that trained them. ONNX Runtime is a small program from Microsoft that runs such files quickly on a CPU, from Python, C++ or C#.

The images are divided into three groups. The model learns from the training group, settings are chosen on the validation group, and the final score comes from the test group, which is used once so the score is not flattering.
When information from the test images reaches training, for example a duplicate image in both groups. The score then looks better than the model really is.
Creating variations of the training images, such as flips and brightness changes, so the model sees more variety than the dataset contains and does not memorise it.
One full pass of the training over all training images. This model was trained for 50.

A range that shows how much a score could move if the test images had been a different sample. It is computed by re-scoring 1,000 random resamples of the test set; here it shows the true mAP is probably between 0.72 and 0.78.
A simple method measured the same way as the model, to show what the model adds. Here it is classical image processing with OpenCV, which scores 0.09 where the model scores 0.79.
A table that shows, for each real defect type, what the model said: the right type, a wrong type, or nothing. Here the errors are misses and false alarms, not wrong names.
A person reviews the cases the model is unsure about and corrects its mistakes. The corrections are kept and used to train the next version.
A different approach that learns only what good parts look like and flags anything unusual. It needs no labelled defects but cannot name the defect type; it was not used here.

An open source licence that requires anyone who distributes or offers software built on the code to publish their own source code too. Ultralytics YOLO uses it and sells a commercial licence to companies that do not want that obligation.
Storing the model's numbers with 8 bits instead of 32 to make it smaller and faster, usually with a small loss of accuracy. It was not applied here and is a next step if more speed is needed.

limits: The model was trained and tested on a public benchmark of 200 by 200 pixel grey images of hot-rolled steel from one source. A real line with its own camera, lighting and material needs new labelled images and retraining.
The dataset has no defect-free images, so the false reject rate on good parts is not measured, and the thresholds were tuned without any clean images.
Two defect types are weak at box level: crazing (AP 0.39) and rolled-in scale (AP 0.53). Crazing alone causes 132 of the 258 false alarms, and its threshold (0.08) is low.

Training stopped at a CPU budget of 50 epochs while the validation score was still rising slowly. It is one run with one seed; the spread between runs was not measured, and no search over training settings was done.
The test set is small (270 images), which is why the scores come with confidence intervals. The split is random, not by production batch, because the dataset has no batch information.

The verdict rule is generic: any confident defect rejects the part. A real acceptance standard depends on defect size and position, which needs the client's rules and a pixel-to-millimetre calibration.
Latency was measured on one small image at a time. A high resolution line camera needs tiling or a larger input, and the speed must be measured again.
Larger models, other detectors and quantisation were not compared, so no claim is made about them.
The review screen has no login, and the review log is a local CSV file with images, not a database.
The model file is AGPL-3.0 because it was trained with Ultralytics YOLO. A closed commercial product needs the Ultralytics Enterprise licence or a retrain with a permissively licensed detector.
The NEU-DET dataset has no stated licence. It is downloaded by a script and not stored in the repository, except twelve sample images kept for the demo and the tests.
Training on CPU is not exactly repeatable across machines, so a retrained model will score close to the published numbers, not identically.

verification.tests: 69 passed in 6.2 seconds with pytest -q, offline. Run twice: in the build environment, and in a fresh environment containing only requirements.txt (no PyTorch, no Ultralytics).
verification.notes: This project uses no language model, so there is no live check and no API cost. The quick start was verified from a fresh virtual environment with only requirements.txt installed: the tests passed, the command line tool inspected the samples, and the server was started, called with curl and driven in headless Chrome to produce docs/screen.png, then stopped. All metrics come from python -m defects.evaluate run on the final exported model. The dataset (88 MB prepared) and the PyTorch weights are not committed; the 10.5 MB ONNX model and twelve sample images are. Licence points to be aware of before pushing: the model file is AGPL-3.0 (stated in the README and model/README.md) and the NEU-DET dataset has no stated licence (twelve sample images are included with attribution).
